# The Rain Ledger

The first leak appeared above the atlases.

It was no more than a brown spot in the library ceiling, shaped a little like an island. Ada noticed it on a Tuesday morning while reshelving a book about rivers. By Thursday, a bead of water hung from the center of the spot. It trembled whenever a truck passed outside.

She put a bucket beneath it and wrote a note to the town’s maintenance office. Then she moved the atlases to a dry shelf.

Two weeks later, the ceiling was still dripping. The bucket had acquired a green line around its inside, and the note had acquired a reference number. Ada knew this because a woman from the office had called to give it to her.

“We have you in the system,” the woman said.

“That’s good,” Ada replied, watching a drop fall into the bucket. “Is there anyone in the system who can fix it?”

The woman laughed before she could stop herself. “I’ll ask.”

Ada had lived in Bellwether long enough to know the difference between a difficult job and a job that had become difficult because nobody had done it when it was small. She was fifty-eight, had spent thirty-one years in the library, and could identify a book’s likely date by the smell of its paper. She also knew the building’s sounds. In the morning its pipes knocked twice before the radiators warmed. In a strong wind, a window on the second floor whistled in a low note. Until that autumn, the roof had never made a sound at all.

The rain came hard on the last Friday of October. Water struck the library windows so fiercely that Ada couldn’t see the clock on the bank across the street. At half past four, the bucket filled. She replaced it with a wastebasket. At five, water began running down the wall behind the atlases, and she called the maintenance office again. It had closed for the day.

She found a roll of plastic sheeting in the supply cupboard. Inez, the library’s newest assistant, helped her carry books away from the wall. They worked quickly, stacking atlases and travel guides on carts.

“Where does it go?” Inez asked.

Ada looked up. “The rain?”

“The water. After it gets through the roof.”

“Anywhere it can.”

Inez put her hand against the wall. “It’s wet over here too.”

They shifted another shelf of books. When they finished, Ada wrote the date, time, and location of each wet patch on the back of an overdue notice. She added the amount of rain reported by the weather station at the school. It was a habit from her father, who had kept careful records of the vegetables he grew. He had written down seeds, planting dates, frost, and harvests. When a row of beans failed, he liked to know whether the same thing had happened before.

On Saturday the rain stopped. Ada went to the library anyway. Daylight showed that water had traveled much farther than she had thought. The carpet was damp beside the history shelves. A patch of plaster had softened near the front desk. She took photographs and sent them to the maintenance office with her reference number in the subject line.

On Monday, a roofer arrived. He climbed a ladder, stayed on the roof for twenty minutes, and came down with a strip of black roofing felt in his hand.

“There’s your trouble,” he said. “Drain’s blocked, and the flashing’s lifted.”

“Can you fix it?”

“I can clear the drain now. Flashing needs a crew. There’s damage under it.”

He made notes on a clipboard. Ada watched the leaves and muddy water spill from the downpipe when he cleared the blockage. The gutter, freed at last, rattled as it emptied.

By the following week the ceiling had dried. No crew had come to repair the flashing.

One afternoon, while Ada was covering a stained atlas in fresh plastic, a boy asked why all the books about oceans were in the local history section.

“Because that’s where we had room,” she said.

He considered this. “Will they stay there?”

“I hope not.”

“Good,” he said. “I thought it was part of a project.”

After he left, Ada opened a notebook and copied in the observations from the overdue notice. The spot above the atlases. The wall. The carpet. The blocked drain. The missing crew. On a page across from them, she wrote the weather station’s figures for the last three storms. She wasn’t sure what she intended to do with them. The notebook made the work feel less likely to disappear.

In November, Inez’s kitchen ceiling began to leak.

She lived above a pharmacy on King Street with her mother and younger brother. Their landlord sent a man who painted over the stain. The paint was white and bright, and for a few days the ceiling looked new. Then a yellow crescent appeared near the light fixture.

Inez told Ada while they were sorting returns. Ada offered her the number of the roofer, then remembered Inez rented the apartment.

“We’ve told the landlord,” Inez said. “My mother’s keeping the emails.”

“Keep photographs too.”

“She is. She photographs everything now. I have to move my dinner so she can photograph the table.”

They smiled, but Ada thought about the white paint for the rest of the day.

At closing, Inez came upon the notebook beside the circulation desk. Ada had been using it to track the library roof. Inez flipped through a few pages.

“You could put my ceiling in here.”

“It’s a different building.”

“It’s still rain.”

Ada gave her the notebook. Inez drew a line beneath the library entries and wrote the date, her address, and *kitchen light fixture*. She added, *Brown water when windy.*

Soon there were more entries. Mrs. Salazar reported water beneath the back door of her shop whenever the street drain filled. A man who came in daily to read the newspapers said the footpath under the railway bridge had flooded three times that month. The music teacher from the primary school mentioned a damp wall in a practice room. Each person knew about one troublesome place. Ada began giving them blank pages to fill in, then copying their notes into the ledger.

Inez suggested a map.

They spread a large street map on a table in the children’s area after closing. It was old enough to show the cinema that had become a car park, but the streets were right. With colored pencils, they marked roof leaks in blue, flooded roads in red, and damp walls in green. By the time they finished, red marks crowded the lower half of town, where the streets ran toward the river.

“That makes sense,” Ada said. “It’s downhill.”

“Look at this,” Inez said. She pointed to three blue marks on King Street, including her apartment. “These are all on the same side.”

Ada leaned closer. The buildings faced an empty lot where a warehouse had been demolished in summer. She knew little about drainage, and the map couldn’t tell her what was happening beneath the ground. Still, she turned to a fresh page and drew a small square for the lot.

In December, the council announced that the lower footpath beside the river would be closed for repairs. It had subsided after repeated flooding. The notice described the work as unexpected.

Ada read the word twice.

At the next council meeting, she and Inez brought the ledger. They arrived early, carrying the map rolled inside a cardboard tube. The meeting room smelled of wet coats. There were twelve chairs for the public, and most were occupied by people who had come to speak about parking.

When Ada’s turn came, she opened the ledger at the first page. She explained about the library roof and the other reports. Inez held up the map. From the front row it looked like a town that had broken out in colored spots.

A councillor thanked them. The facilities manager said the library roof was scheduled for inspection. The chair asked whether the map could be emailed.

“It can,” Inez said. She had already photographed it.

Ada asked about the river footpath. She pointed to the dates people had recorded water crossing it.

“We’ve been monitoring that site,” the facilities manager said.

“I’m glad,” Ada replied. “I thought these might be useful.”

On the walk home, Inez was quiet.

“We got an inspection,” Ada said.

“We got one before we went in. He told us it was scheduled.”

Ada carried the ledger against her coat. She had hoped to leave it with someone, but nobody had asked for it.

The next rain was forecast for the week before Christmas. The school weather station predicted a strong storm, and people came to the library for books and films to take home. Ada noticed that Mrs. Salazar had taped a piece of clear plastic across the bottom of her shop door. At King Street, Inez and her mother moved a table away from the kitchen light.

The storm began at night. At six the next morning, Inez called Ada.

“There’s water in the hall,” she said. “It’s coming down the stairs.”

“Are you all right?”

“We’re outside. Mrs. Salazar let us into the shop.”

Ada pulled on boots and a raincoat. The streets were dim and nearly empty. Water rushed along the gutters, carrying leaves, a paper cup, and one small yellow ball. At the library she found a new drip above the atlases. She set a bucket beneath it, then walked to King Street.

The empty lot was a shallow lake. At its far edge stood a temporary fence and a mound of earth left by the demolition crew. Water ran from the lot onto the pavement, gathering around a blocked drain before reaching the pharmacy building. The shop’s cellar steps had filled. In the upstairs hall, water dripped through a ceiling fixture onto the carpet.

A fire crew arrived and turned off the electricity. They checked each apartment and helped the residents carry out what they could. Inez brought down a bag of clothes, her brother’s school notebooks, and a pan of bread dough their mother had made the night before. She held the pan level beneath her coat.

“Couldn’t leave it,” she said.

Ada drove them to her house. While Inez’s mother called their landlord, Ada put the dough near the radiator. It rose unevenly, higher on one side. They baked it anyway and ate thick slices at the kitchen table.

Later, when the rain weakened, Inez opened her laptop. She had photographed the lot after three earlier storms. In the first picture, water stood among the weeds. In the second, it reached the foot of the fence. In the third, it spread across the pavement.

“My mother said it would come in one day,” she said. “She called about it.”

They found the emails. They added them to a folder with the pictures, the ledger pages, and the weather station readings. Inez’s mother supplied photographs of the ceiling stain beneath its fresh paint. Ada wrote a short account of what she had seen that morning and gave the names of the people who could confirm it.

By evening, Mrs. Salazar had sent a picture of water entering her shop. The music teacher sent records of damp in the practice room, which backed onto King Street. Other residents contributed photographs of the lot from their windows. Some disagreed about where the water was coming from. One had noticed a blocked street drain; another thought the demolished warehouse had once had its own drainage channel. Ada kept both accounts. They had names and dates, and someone with the right plans could check them.

The local paper published a short article two days later. A reporter had spoken with the residents and the council. The council said an engineer would inspect the lot and the street drains. The landlord said repairs to the apartments would begin when the building was dry enough.

During the first week of January, an engineer in an orange jacket came to the library. His name was Mr. Vale, and he asked to see the map. Inez happened to be working, so she unrolled it across the returns counter while Ada brought out the ledger.

Vale studied the colored marks for a long time. Then he asked if he could take a photograph. He pointed to the empty lot.

“The warehouse had a drain here,” he said. “It connected to a culvert running under King Street. We’re checking what happened to the connection when they took the building down.”

“Will that fix the roof?” Ada asked.

He looked at the blue marks. “Which roof?”

“That was partly a joke.”

He grinned, then grew serious. He said the street drain had been blocked, but that clearing it would not be enough if water from the lot kept flowing toward the buildings. He did not yet know whether the old culvert was damaged or filled in. He wrote down several dates from the ledger and asked Inez to send him her photographs.

A week later, contractors dug a trench at the edge of the lot. They found the old connection capped at the wrong point. The demolition plans had shown where it ought to be, but the pipe itself had taken a different route. During heavy rain, water that had once drained away collected against the mound of earth and spilled onto King Street.

The contractors installed a new channel and cleared the street drains. The council sent residents a letter explaining the work. A roofer came to the library too, with a crew this time. He repaired the flashing, replaced water-damaged boards, and made Ada climb halfway up the ladder so he could show her that the roof drain was clear.

“I’ll believe you from here,” she said, gripping the rung.

“You wanted to know it was done.”

“I do. I also want to get down.”

By February, the apartments above the pharmacy had dried enough for repairs to begin. Inez and her family were staying with an aunt across town. Their landlord had not become easier to deal with, but the fire crew’s report and the photographs made it harder for him to claim the damage was a stain that needed paint. Mrs. Salazar reopened the back half of her shop. The primary school moved its music lessons out of the damp room while its wall was repaired.

One clear morning, Ada took the ledger off her desk and put it in the local history section. She left a pen beside it and a note inside the cover: *For reports of rain entering places it should not.*

The first new entry was in a child’s handwriting. *Water comes through the bus shelter roof by the park. It gets on the seat. Tuesday, 8:10 a.m.*

Ada drew a small blue mark on the map. Then she phoned the transit office. The person who answered gave her a reference number and said a crew would inspect the shelter.

She wrote the number beside the child’s entry. She had learned that it was worth keeping both.
